title: JESUS SAID TO TEAR OUT YOUR EYE AND CUT OFF YOUR HAND. WHAT WAS HE REALLY TRYING TO SAVE YOU FROM?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID TO TEAR OUT YOUR EYE AND CUT OFF YOUR HAND. WHAT WAS HE REALLY TRYING TO SAVE YOU FROM?

The terrifying warning in Matthew 5:29–30 that many Christians misunderstand—and the breathtaking mercy hidden inside the words of a Savior who would rather confront your sin than watch it destroy you.
There are words Jesus spoke that comfort the broken.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Matthew 11:28, KJV)
There are words that bring peace to the frightened.
“Let not your heart be troubled.” (John 14:1, KJV)
And then there are words so severe, so unsettling, that even people who have followed Jesus for years sometimes read them quickly, hoping to reach a gentler passage.
Words like these:
“And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.
“And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.”
—Matthew 5:29–30, KJV
Read that again.
Not because Jesus wants you to hurt yourself.
He does not.
But because there is something in those words that our comfortable Christianity desperately needs to hear.
Jesus, the One who healed blind eyes, spoke about tearing an eye out.
Jesus, the One who restored broken bodies, spoke about cutting off a hand.
Jesus, the One who welcomed sinners, warned them about hell.
Why?
What could possibly be so dangerous that the Son of God would use language this shocking?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is this:
What if the thing Jesus is warning you about is something you have already learned to excuse?
Something you protect.
Something you return to when nobody is watching.
Something you keep calling a weakness even though, deep down, you know it has become a master.
Stay with these words.
Because by the time we reach the cross, you may discover that this passage is not about a Savior demanding your blood.
It is about a Savior who shed His own blood to rescue you from sin—and who loves you too much to tell you that the sin destroying you is harmless.
Picture an ordinary evening.
The house is quiet. Everyone else is asleep.
A man reaches for his phone.
He knows exactly where his thumb is going.
He has promised God he would stop.
He has cried about it before. Deleted things before. Made commitments before.
Yet there he is again, standing at the same doorway, preparing to walk back into the same darkness.
Another woman sits alone, scrolling through the life of someone she secretly resents.
She smiles at that person in public.
She even prays for them when others are listening.
But privately, she feeds the bitterness.
Another believer opens a conversation that should have ended months ago.
“It is innocent,” they whisper.
“We are just friends.”
But the heart knows when a boundary is being crossed long before the mouth is willing to confess it.
Different people.
Different temptations.
The same terrifying pattern.
We do not always fall into sin because we cannot see the danger.
Sometimes we fall because we have become skilled at negotiating with it.
And Jesus refuses to negotiate.
To understand why, we must return to the mountainside where He first spoke these words.
In Matthew 5, Jesus is delivering what we now call the Sermon on the Mount.
He is revealing the righteousness of God's kingdom.
Not a righteousness built on religious appearances, but one that reaches into the heart.
Just before His warning about the eye and the hand, Jesus says something that would have deeply challenged His listeners.
“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery:
“But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
—Matthew 5:27–28, KJV
Jesus is not saying that every passing awareness of another person's beauty is adultery.
Nor is He condemning someone merely for experiencing an unwanted temptation.
The language concerns a gaze directed toward lust—a look that deliberately cultivates sexual desire outside God's righteous boundaries.
And suddenly, the issue is no longer merely what someone has done physically.
It is what someone is choosing to entertain inwardly.
A person may never have crossed the physical boundary of adultery and still be nurturing unfaithfulness in the heart.
A person may look respectable in church while privately feeding desires that contradict the faithfulness they profess.
That is why the warning comes immediately afterward.
If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out.
If your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off.
But did Jesus actually command His followers to mutilate their bodies?
No.
The passage uses shocking, deliberately forceful imagery to communicate the seriousness of dealing with sin. It is not an instruction to injure yourself.
And the original Greek helps us see the force of His warning.
The expression translated “causes you to sin” is connected to the Greek verb σκανδαλίζω (skandalizō).
In Matthew 5:29, the phrase is:
σκανδαλίζει σε — skandalizei se
Meaning, in this context, “causes you to stumble” or “causes you to sin.”
The word belongs to a family of terms associated with stumbling, offense, and entrapment.
This is not simply about something that annoys you or makes you uncomfortable.
Jesus is speaking about something that becomes an occasion for moral and spiritual stumbling.
Something that draws you toward disobedience.
Something that threatens to pull your heart away from the path of righteousness.
Notice the brilliance of His illustration.
He mentions the right eye and the right hand.
The eye represents something precious and useful, and in this immediate context, it is especially relevant to the lustful gaze.
The hand is likewise an essential instrument of ordinary life and action.
Jesus chooses parts of the body that people naturally value.
His point is not that the body itself is evil.
His point is that even something precious must never be treated as more important than obedience to God.
And that changes everything.
Because sometimes the greatest spiritual danger is not something we openly hate.
Sometimes it is something we deeply enjoy.
Something familiar.
Something convenient.
Something we have convinced ourselves we cannot live without.
The relationship that repeatedly leads us into compromise.
The private account we use to hide what we would never display publicly.
The conversations that awaken desires we should not cultivate.
The entertainment we keep consuming even though we know what it does to our minds.
The secret habit that has become part of our nightly routine.
And here is the question we would rather avoid:
If we know something repeatedly leads us toward sin, why do we keep making room for it?
We say we want freedom.
But sometimes we keep the door unlocked.
We ask God to deliver us from temptation while preserving the very arrangements that make temptation easier to pursue.
We pray for purity but refuse to establish boundaries.
We ask for healing but continue feeding the wound.
And Jesus says, with a seriousness that cannot be softened into a motivational quote:
Remove what is leading you into sin.
Not your literal eye.
Not your literal hand.
Remove the access.
Remove the invitation.
Remove the opportunity you have been deliberately protecting.
If an application repeatedly becomes a doorway to pornography, remove the application or establish meaningful safeguards.
If a relationship is drawing you into unfaithfulness, establish the necessary boundaries, even if that means ending the relationship.
If certain conversations repeatedly lead to destructive behavior, stop participating in them.
If secrecy has become the environment in which your sin grows, bring the struggle into the light with a trustworthy, mature believer or pastor.
And if a harmful pattern has become compulsive or deeply entrenched, seek appropriate professional support alongside spiritual care.
Because radical repentance is not measured by how dramatically you punish yourself.
It is demonstrated by how seriously you turn away from sin and toward Christ.
But there is another truth here that we cannot afford to miss.
Jesus is not teaching that an eye or a hand is the ultimate source of human sinfulness.
In Mark 7:20–23, He explains that evil thoughts and sinful actions proceed from within the human heart.
Removing a body part would not remove the heart's capacity to desire evil.
That is one reason a literal interpretation of self-mutilation fails to understand His teaching.
A person could lose an eye and still lust.
A person could lose a hand and still hate.
A person could suffer terribly in the body and remain unchanged in the heart.
Jesus is calling for decisive repentance, not bodily destruction.
And that leads us to something even more frightening than the imagery itself.
The word translated “hell.”
In Matthew 5:29–30, the Greek word is γέεννα (Gehenna).

Gehenna is derived from the name of the Valley of Hinnom, associated in the Old Testament with horrific idolatrous practices, including child sacrifice, and later used in Jewish religious language in connection with divine judgment.
In Jesus' teaching, Gehenna serves as a grave warning about final judgment.
We should not reduce it to mere embarrassment, temporary regret, or an unpleasant consequence.
Jesus is speaking about eternal realities.
And He is making a comparison.
Better to surrender something valuable now than to cling to sin at the expense of something infinitely greater.
But be careful here.
Jesus is not teaching that salvation can be purchased through suffering, self-denial, or sufficiently severe religious discipline.
The same New Testament declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
“Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
—Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by mutilating ourselves, performing religious achievements, or accumulating enough good behavior to cancel our guilt.
Yet the grace that saves us is not permission to remain comfortably enslaved to sin.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's saving grace also trains believers to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace does not merely pardon.
Grace also transforms.
And genuine repentance is not the price we pay to purchase God's mercy.
It is part of our response to the mercy that calls us back to Him.
Think about Peter.
The disciple who confidently declared that he would never abandon Jesus.
The man who believed his loyalty was stronger than the pressure around him.
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
The denials.
And finally, the rooster.
Luke 22:61 records one of the most heartbreaking moments in Scripture:
“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.”
Imagine that look.
The man who had promised never to deny Jesus had just denied Him three times.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
But that was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, in John 21, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
Peter's failure was real.
His repentance mattered.
And Christ's mercy was greater than the shame of his collapse.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sin was harmless.
Not that denial did not matter.
Not that Peter could continue living in rebellion without consequence.
But that the risen Christ was able to restore a man who had fallen terribly.
Perhaps that is why this passage hurts.
Because some of us recognize ourselves in Peter.
We know what it means to promise God something sincerely and then fail.
We know what it means to worship on Sunday while struggling with temptation on Monday.
We know the strange exhaustion of asking forgiveness for something we had already asked forgiveness for before.
We know what it means to feel ashamed of our own inconsistency.
And after enough failures, a dangerous thought begins to whisper:
Maybe this is simply who I am.
Maybe I will never change.
Maybe God is tired of hearing me repent.
But listen carefully.
Your struggle does not give you permission to surrender to sin.
And your failure does not mean Christ is unwilling to receive a repentant sinner.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The promise is not that believers will never face temptation.
The promise is that forgiveness and cleansing are found in the faithful and righteous God who receives those who confess their sins.
And Romans 8:1 announces:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That is not an invitation to become careless about holiness.
It is a reason to stop hiding and return to the Savior.
Because condemnation and conviction are not the same thing.
Conviction exposes sin and calls us toward repentance.
Condemnation leaves us believing that hope is gone.
The Gospel tells us that the believer's hope rests not in flawless personal performance but in Jesus Christ.
And now we arrive at the most beautiful contrast in this entire passage.
Jesus warned His followers about the danger of sin using the imagery of losing an eye or a hand.
But when the hour came for humanity's redemption, He did not demand that sinners mutilate themselves to earn forgiveness.
He went to the cross.
His hands were pierced.
His body was wounded.
His blood was shed.
Not because His followers could save themselves through their own suffering.
But because they could not.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
In its prophetic context, Isaiah speaks of the suffering servant who bears the sins of others. Christians understand this passage as finding its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
And 1 Peter 2:24 speaks directly of Christ:
“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.”
Do you see it?
The Savior who warned us to take sin seriously is the same Savior who bore our sins upon the cross.
He did not minimize the disease.
He came to accomplish the cure.
He did not pretend judgment was imaginary.
He gave Himself so that sinners could be reconciled to God.
He did not come merely to improve our religious reputation.
He came to save us.
And when Jesus cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30), He announced the completion of His saving work on the cross.
The Greek word recorded there is τετέλεσται (tetelestai), from the verb teleō, meaning to finish, complete, or bring to its intended end.
In John's account, it is a declaration that Jesus' appointed work had reached its fulfillment.
We should not reduce this profound statement to a simplistic slogan about every personal struggle disappearing immediately.
Christ's redemptive work is complete.
Our growth in holiness continues as we follow Him.
That distinction matters.
Because you may genuinely belong to Christ and still be fighting temptations that once dominated your life.
You may be learning obedience through painful decisions.
You may need accountability, patience, prayer, Scripture, wise counsel, and repeated acts of turning away from what once controlled you.
Sanctification is not always instantaneous.
Sometimes it looks like deleting the number.
Sometimes it looks like confessing the truth.
Sometimes it looks like apologizing to someone you wounded.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to open the door you used to walk through without thinking.
Sometimes it looks like falling to your knees after another failure, not to bargain with God, but to return honestly to the mercy of Christ.
And sometimes the most spiritually courageous thing you can say is:
“Lord, I cannot keep pretending this is harmless.”
That is where repentance becomes personal.
Not in the performance of appearing holy.
But in the surrender of the places where we have resisted God.
There is a reason Jesus speaks so forcefully in Matthew 5.
He knows that sin is deceptive.
Hebrews 3:13 speaks of “the deceitfulness of sin.”
Sin rarely introduces itself by announcing the destruction it intends.
It often arrives disguised as relief.
As comfort.
As companionship.
As entertainment.
As revenge that feels justified.
As a secret that supposedly hurts nobody.
And by the time its consequences become visible, the heart may already have learned to defend what once disturbed the conscience.
This is why the warnings of Jesus are merciful.
Not comfortable.
Merciful.
A physician who discovers a life-threatening condition does not demonstrate compassion by pretending nothing is wrong.
Love tells the truth.
And the perfect love of Christ tells us the truth about sin while offering the grace we desperately need.
But here is where we must also be careful with ourselves and others.
Not every painful emotion is evidence of personal sin.
Not every intrusive thought is something a person has chosen.
Not every experience of temptation is itself an act of disobedience.
Hebrews 4:15 teaches that Jesus was tempted, yet without sin.
Someone struggling with unwanted thoughts, anxiety, or obsessive religious fears should not interpret this passage as a command to harm themselves or punish their bodies.
Jesus' teaching calls for repentance from sin, not violence against the person God created.
The answer to sin is not self-hatred.
It is turning to Christ.
The answer to temptation is not destroying your body.
It is seeking God's help and making wise, faithful choices.
And the answer to repeated failure is not despair.
It is honest confession, repentance, and continued dependence upon the Savior.
Perhaps someone reading this has been hiding for a very long time.
Not because you do not believe in God.
You do.
Not because you have never experienced His goodness.
You have.
But because there is one particular area of your life that you have carefully kept beyond the reach of surrender.
You have given Jesus your worship songs.
Your Sunday attendance.
Your public testimony.
Your religious language.
But there is a private room in your heart where you still insist on keeping the key.
And today, His words are reaching that room.
Not to humiliate you.
Not to make you believe that you are beyond redemption.
But to call you out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
What if the next step in your spiritual life is not another emotional promise?
What if it is one honest act of obedience?
One confession.
One boundary.
One conversation.
One decision to stop feeding what is weakening your walk with God.
Jesus said in John 8:36:
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”
Freedom is not found in pretending temptation does not exist.
Freedom is found in the Son of God.
And walking in that freedom means learning to reject what once held us captive.
This is not easy.
Sometimes obedience costs us something we genuinely enjoy.
Sometimes it costs a relationship.
Sometimes it costs approval.
Sometimes it means losing access to something that has become part of our daily routine.
But Jesus never promised that following Him would require nothing.
He said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.”
—Luke 9:23, KJV
Daily.
Not merely when the music is playing.
Not only when the sermon is moving.
Not only when someone is watching.
Daily.
And the beautiful thing about following Jesus is that the call to surrender comes from the One who first gave Himself for us.
He is not asking you to earn a place in His heart through religious suffering.
He is calling you to trust Him more than the sin that promises satisfaction and leaves you empty.
Not because a writer has demanded your attention.
But because the words of Jesus deserve more than a passing glance.
If this passage has exposed a struggle you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers the details.
But perhaps you can take one honest step today.
You can pray.
You can confess.
You can seek help.
You can tell a trusted believer that you need accountability.
Not as a performance.
Not as a public display of your private wounds.
But as a simple confession that you still need the grace of Jesus.
And if Christ has already brought you through a season of bondage, perhaps your testimony can encourage someone who thinks freedom is impossible.
Someone reading those words may realize that they are not the only person learning to walk in repentance.
Someone may find courage to seek help.
Someone may finally believe that failure does not have to be the final chapter.
There may come another evening when temptation feels stronger than your resolve.
Another moment when compromise begins to sound reasonable.
Another day when you need to remember why Jesus spoke with such urgency.
Return to His words.
Return to Scripture.
Return to the truth that what promises a moment of pleasure may carry consequences far beyond that moment.
Not merely to increase its reach.
Someone who loves Jesus but feels trapped.
Someone who has mistaken repeated failure for hopelessness.
Someone who thinks repentance means God has stopped loving them.
Someone who has never understood why the Gospel confronts sin so seriously while offering mercy so freely.
You never know which conversation may become an opportunity for someone to return to Jesus.
And if you have been walking with Gospel Warrior for a while, you already know that our mission is not simply to publish another Christian article.
We want to help people open their Bibles, understand the Gospel, confront sin honestly, grow in discipleship, and discover that their past does not have to define their future.
We believe biblical nourishment should reach people who are hungry for truth, including those who cannot afford to purchase books or other resources.
But continuing and expanding this work also requires practical support.
And please hear this clearly.
You do not need to give money to receive His forgiveness.
But if God has placed this work on your heart, supporting it can be one meaningful expression of generosity and partnership in sharing the Gospel.
These products are not the reason to follow Jesus, and they are not spiritual rewards.
They are simply a way for us to express appreciation to those who help sustain this mission.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the person who has grown spiritually cold.
Invite the seeker who has questions about Jesus.
Even invite the person who does not yet believe, because the Gospel is not reserved for those who already know the answers.
Sometimes the most important thing we can do with a message is not simply agree with it.
It is allow the truth to change us—and then faithfully pass it on.
But before you leave, return with me one final time to the mountainside.
Jesus is standing before the crowd.
He has spoken about adultery.
About lust.
About the heart.
About the eye.
About the hand.
About judgment.
And His words have left no room for pretending that sin is a harmless game.
Now imagine listening to those words with the full knowledge of what would happen later.
The betrayal.
The arrest.
The mockery.
The crown of thorns.
The nails.
The cross.
The tomb.
And then the resurrection.
The One who spoke the warning would Himself become the sacrifice.
The One who exposed the darkness would open the way to forgiveness.
The One who called sinners to repentance would give His life to save them.
This is why Matthew 5:29–30 should not leave us fascinated with the frightening image of a severed hand or a missing eye.
It should leave us asking a far more important question.
If Jesus took my sin seriously enough to die for it, why would I continue treating it as something harmless?
Not because I am trying to earn His love.
But because His love is too precious to keep answering with deliberate compromise.
Not because I am beyond mercy.
But because mercy is calling me into a different way of living.
Not because I can save myself.
But because Jesus Christ has done what I could never do.
And perhaps tonight, somewhere in the quiet of your own heart, there is a decision waiting to be made.
Not a dramatic announcement.
Not a religious performance.
Just a surrender.

“Lord Jesus, I have defended what You have called me to leave behind. I have made excuses where I needed repentance. Forgive me. Change my heart. Give me wisdom to remove what draws me into sin, courage to seek help where I need it, and faith to keep following You. Thank You for bearing my sins on the cross and for rising again. Teach me to love You more than the things that compete for my obedience. Amen.”
And when you finish praying, do not assume the next step must be spectacular.
It may be small.
It may be private.
It may be difficult.
But take it.
Because the Gospel is not merely the story of how Jesus forgives what we have done.
It is also the story of how His grace begins to change who we are becoming.
You are not saved by cutting off your hand.
You are not redeemed by tearing out your eye.
You are saved through Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for sinners and calls those who follow Him to turn from sin and walk in newness of life.
And here is the truth I hope stays with you long after this article disappears from your screen:
The sin you are afraid to surrender can never love you the way the Savior who died to free you already has.
